slides.title: Module 2 review: tissues
bullets: A tissue is a complex of cells and intercellular substance specialised for a particular structure and function; main types: epithelial, internal-environment tissues (blood, connective), muscle and nervous.
The classification is relative: the main criterion is structure and function, not origin from a germ layer.
An organ has a stroma (framework) and a parenchyma (the tissue doing the main function); many cells rest on a basement membrane.

Epithelium: avascular, on a basement membrane, regenerates well; types — simple (squamous, cuboidal, columnar), pseudostratified, stratified (non-keratinised, keratinised), transitional; glandular epithelium — merocrine, apocrine, holocrine secretion.
Connective tissue develops from mesoderm; its cells lie singly in an intercellular substance (ground substance and collagen, elastic, reticular fibres); blood is one of its forms.

slides.title: Module 2 review: tissues
bullets: Collagen and elastin are the main structural proteins of connective tissue.

slides.title: An organ example: kidney structure and urine formation
bullets: The urinary organs are two kidneys, the ureters, the bladder and the urethra; the kidney is a paired bean-shaped organ made of cortex and medulla.
The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the nephron (more than 1 million in each kidney).

Nephron: the glomerulus (Malpighian tuft) enclosed by the Shumlyansky–Bowman capsule (podocytes and basement membrane), proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct.

Urine forms in three steps: filtration (plasma is filtered in the glomerulus into the capsule space — primary urine; high-molecular proteins such as fibrinogen do not pass), reabsorption (water and needed substances return to the blood — secondary urine) and secretion (tubular epithelium actively releases ammonia, drugs, H⁺, HCO₃⁻ and others).

slides.title: An organ example: kidney structure and urine formation
bullets: According to the book, 150–180 L of primary urine form per day and shrink to 1.2–1.8 L of secondary urine after reabsorption.
Urine consists of about 96% water, 1.5% salts and 2.5% organic substances (urea, uric acid and others).

Theory of urine formation?
bullets: 1. Urine is formed in the nephron: filtration in the glomeruli (primary urine – protein-free ultrafiltrate of plasma, ~180 L per day), reabsorption and secretion in the tubules, concentration in the collecting ducts.
2. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the main indicator of kidney function; in practice eGFR is calculated from creatinine (and cystatin C).

3. Proximal tubule: glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate, Na and most of the water are reabsorbed; loop of Henle – concentration gradient via the countercurrent mechanism; distal tubule and collecting ducts – final regulation under aldosterone (Na/K) and ADH (water).
4. Laboratory reflection: glucosuria (if filtered glucose exceeds reabsorption capacity), proteinuria (glomerular or tubular damage), urine density/osmolality (concentrating ability).
5. Kidney disease is classified by KDIGO by eGFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3).

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 1. Physical properties: amount (in adults ~600–2000 mL/day), color (bilirubin, blood, hemoglobin/myoglobin, drugs), clarity (turbidity – salts, leukocytes, bacteria, mucus), odor, relative density (1.002–1.035; urinometer, refractometer or test strip) – renal concentrating ability.

2. Chemical examination – test strips: pH (4.5–8), protein (mainly albumin; alkaline pH – false positive), glucose (when the reabsorption threshold is exceeded), ketones (acetoacetate/acetone, β-hydroxybutyrate is not detected), blood (erythrocytes, hemoglobin, myoglobin – peroxidase activity), leukocyte esterase, nitrites (some bacteria), bilirubin, urobilinogen.
3. Interferences: ascorbate (false negative blood, glucose, nitrite, leukocyte esterase), concentrated or dilute urine, drugs (phenazopyridine).

slides.title: Examining the physical and chemical properties of urine?
bullets: 4. Confirmatory tests: for protein – sulfosalicylic acid (all proteins) and quantitative UPCR/ACR, for blood – microscopy, glucose and ketones in blood.
5. Preanalytics: midstream, morning urine, analysis within 1 hour or storage at 4 °C.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 1. Preparation: 5–12 mL of well-mixed fresh urine, centrifuged at ~400×g for 5 minutes, resuspended in a standard volume; under a coverslip at low (×100) and high (×400) magnification; phase contrast/staining, polarization for crystals.

2. Organized elements: erythrocytes (normal 0–5/field; dysmorphic erythrocytes and acanthocytes – glomerular source), leukocytes (0–5; many – infection, inflammation), epithelium (squamous, transitional, renal tubular), casts.

3. Casts: hyaline (a few are normal; concentrated urine, exertion), erythrocyte (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis), leukocyte (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis), granular (tubular damage), waxy (severe CKD), fatty (nephrotic syndrome).
4. Unorganized elements: crystals (oxalates, urates, uric acid, triple phosphates – infection; cystine – cystinuria), bacteria, fungi, trichomonads, sperm.

slides.title: Urine sediment microscopy?
bullets: 5. Automated urine particle analyzers (flow cytometry, digital imaging) – screening; abnormal results are confirmed by microscopy; the result is standardized per unit volume (/µL).
